Information since the prior meeting points to solid growth and ongoing labor-market strength, with core inflation still soft and longer-term expectations little changed. The October Beige Book reports widespread labor shortages—especially in construction and transportation—that are restraining some business growth even as they put upward pressure on wages. Hurricane impacts (Harvey and Irma) in the Richmond, Atlanta, and Dallas Districts disrupted activity but recovery and rebuilding have supported near-term demand and exacerbated labor tightness. Household/retail spending increased across districts. Incorporating the October 2017 SLOOS, banks eased standards for C&I loans (often due to competition) but tightened terms on credit card and auto loans, and saw weaker demand for several business purposes; tightening was motivated by economic outlook, portfolio quality, and lower risk tolerance. Netting these factors, business credit supply remains available, but labor and capacity constraints plus somewhat tighter consumer credit and softer loan demand temper the outlook relative to the headline FOMC statement. Holding rates while signaling gradual hikes and continuing balance-sheet normalization remains consistent with these conditions.
